correctness.rationale: The lower bound comes from two outgoing arcs sharing all predecessors. At equality, domination of every omitted arc forces one selected incoming and outgoing arc at each lower-order vertex, hence a cycle cover. Exactly its two-cycles cause coincident two-element signatures. At n>=4 the three digons constrain disjoint pairs of local line-graph switches, each allowing three of four assignments; n=3 admits only zero or one backtracking base switch. The all-order count and explicit uniform sampler follow. Verified by standard-library enumeration at n=2,3,4,5 and a separately written C++ graph/signature verifier at n=3,4,5; all relative package sources are rerunnable.

originality.rationale: The 2014 de Bruijn full-text bounds and the 2020 Kautz line-digraph thesis give related minimum-size and code-recognition criteria, but neither inspected treatment provides a closed enumeration of all labeled optimum codes at all orders or a uniform rejection-free sampler. The new switch-exclusion count (including two genuinely different small-order exceptions) is an additional result. Priority outside the inspected corpus remains a risk.
residual_risks: A 2020 thesis gives a general arc-code characterization from which the counting question may be derivable; the claimed advance is the explicit all-order enumerator and uniform sampler, not the minimum cardinality.
Other unpublished or unindexed treatments of restricted Kautz cycle covers could precede the enumeration.
The first-source date refers to the checked 2014 source establishing the research setting, not a publication date for this new finding.

value.rationale: The family is a standard low-diameter interconnection network and the smallest identifying codes minimize sensor count. A closed expression for the entire optimum design space, including exceptional short orders, and exact uniform generation answer natural algorithmic counting/sampling questions without brute-force search. The three independent short-cycle exclusions are structural rather than an arbitrary finite slice; this is separate from the previously known optimum size. The scope is exactly radius-one ternary Kautz and no broader performance claim is made.
